Larry Gold

Musician, arranger, and composer Larry Gold has played an integral role in multiple genres of music. His collaboration skills and progressive thinking enabled him to guide hit-making artists from the Philly Sound to current hip hop artists.
Larry was interviewed via Zoom on June 18, 2025 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive, and I'm very pleased to have Larry Gold with me today, musician, arranger, composer, studio owner, and I'm going to describe you as the musical glue in a long line of hit records.
I'll take that.
You'll take that.
I'll take that.
Okay. I'm trying to think of an anecdote, oh yes, this is a little odd. I've been watching re—runs of "The Sopranos."

Me too. I just finished as a matter of fact and it's like — it's my second time without my wife to watch it. And what I do is I actually play the cello — I know the dialogue a lot now so I will play scales and I'll play, you know I'm like working on a few new pieces. My hands hurt. But I'm trying my best you know, with my time, you know I make myself work on music for three or four hours a day no matter what the day may entail like I did when I was little. I mean, you know,
There was character called Christopher, you know Christopher, and there's one session/episode where —
He mentions the "Philly Sound."
Yeah. He mentions the Philly Sound and he was like, "Well I know music —" blah blah blah, and he mentions the Philly Sound.

Well actually what he says was, "The mob's been tied in to the record business forever and he starts mentioning certain names and everything and then he throws in the Philly Sound, which believe it or not, and I'm not going to say it, but the only mob activity the Philly Sound had was via Columbia Records. © Fillius Jazz Archive 2

That's priceless. I don't want to go too far back because we have to end up in the present but I brought in a couple of props today, thinking about your writing, when it occurred and here's my first prop. Score pads.
Yeah. I still have them right here.
Yeah. Did you — you started out that way? Pen and pencil I would imagine?
Absolutely.
Yeah.

Well I went to Curtis so I grew up writing. You know we used to have to imitate Bach chorales and things like that so I was very familiar. But then that whole pop music scene in Philadelphia in the '60s and '70s overwhelmingly fascinated me. You know I mean because they were kids who grew up in my neighborhood after the great songwriters and the great arrangers and the great everybody and it just fascinated me. I went a little different left, I went to Curtis as a cello player but yet participated in Cameo and Parkway and the early Gamble records, and all those early records from I would say from age 14 — 13, 14 on.

I don't want to make too much out of this but it seems to me when you were making this decision at 17 according to your promo here, that you had one foot in the white world of music and you had another in the black world of music. Were you aware of that? Was that partly your decision to go — to leave Curtis and go in this other direction?

Well you know at that moment it was the hippie days so I was playing in a few bands. The bands were based on blues. Blues obviously the derivative of blues is black music, the church the old work songs, every — all that. You know? So yeah I was fascinated. I was also fascinated by popular music in general. But in Philadelphia the people that were really adept that I met were people like Leon Huff and people like, you know they were Tommy Bell and they were really crazily talented people that weren't talented like the fiddle players at Curtis, like the violinists at Curtis, but in a whole different way off the top of their head and involving the black church and a lot of things. It was fascinating. Plus I grew up in a very poor neighborhood. My father had a hardware toy store in North Philly, which was a very mixed neighborhood to begin with. So yes I knew that I had, in those days I don't think today — if you're a classical musician, you go to Juilliard, you can come out and frame your classical background or your jazz background in a whole lot of different light than you used to be able to in the '60s. It's a different world today than it was then. You either had to go one route, the long hair route, which was classical music or you had to go the other route which was almost giving that up. Curtis hated that I used to play at the Latin Casino to make a buck. You know? I mean in those days if I made a few hundred dollars a week that was amazing. I could live forever on it. © Fillius Jazz Archive 3
Playing the bass, right?
Cello.
Playing the cello.
In the string section.
In the string sections. Okay. But you became a bass player.

I did play bass too, and I played guitar too. But I gave them up when, in the '70s, when the '70s really started rolling and I started arranging and making records and doing all that stuff I didn't play the bass anymore. I barely played the cello anymore.
On average, when you were hired to write string charts, can you describe the tracks that were given to you? Did it have the vocals on it usually or was it just the basic rhythm section?

It had a rhythm section and vocals. Almost 95% of the time it had vocals and a rhythm section. Every once in a while it might not have had backgrounds on it but a lot of them before the arranger got the record they were almost finished.
Which is a challenge in itself, isn't it? The ability to know what not to write as well as what to write.

You just hit the nail on the head as we say. The thing is is that when a record is almost done there's not much room for you to overwrite. I mean you really have to pick your spots. And in my whole life, all these sixty years I'm picking my spots. You know? Yeah. I mean, and I have the tendency to be in a more simple way than a lot of other arrangers. I don't like over—do things. I like things to be poignant and emotional, you know. If it's a great R&B record I like to make it an R&B opera. You know? Give it that background where the height of the record hits its peak and then trails off and does its thing.
What's your preferred string section? If you have a decent budget do you like — how many violins violas, etcetera?

Well it all depends. In the old days I had six violins, two violas, and two cellos, which I still do a lot today. And much against union rules, I double that. And even back in the '70s and the '60s I used to double that. So, and that to me, if I get a couple of great performances that's plenty.
Did your string players, when you were overdubbing and doubling did they like to hear what they just played in their headphones?
Sometimes yes, some of them would, and sometimes no.
Okay.

You know when I first started playing on records we didn't even have earphones. We used little speakers. There was a speaker in the room and everybody just could hear each other. And then I guess when we doubled it they reversed the phase on or something © Fillius Jazz Archive 4

somehow they canceled out the speaker. And the speaker couldn't be really loud so there was usually one speaker in front of the cellos and violas and maybe one speaker to the side of the violins, and maybe one to the other side. And that was the way, all through the '60s that's how we did it in Philadelphia.
It must have contributed, even marginally to the sound of those records because you're recording the room on the overdub even though you might have been trying to avoid it, you're still getting that.

I think you're right, you know I think you're right. You know Phil Ramone came down late '70s one time to record something. And I was playing that time, and I even think I helped him get the section together. And he said, he couldn't believe how small Sigma was. The ceilings weren't very high. The room dimension was really small. He was used to big rooms you know. I mean but he was amazed that Joe Tarsia got that great sound from such a small room.

I thought of a comment. Recently I interviewed Alan Broadbent and I asked him what it was like the very first time you write something and you hear it played. And he described it as a "cringe moment." Because you never quite now how it's going to lay until they really start to play it.

Well especially in the '70s and the '80s before we had all these computers. Now I can do a little dubbing, I have a Synclavier so I can put the song in my Synclavier and do a little sketch and I can listen to it. It's not the same at all but at least I can hear — I can play with the voicing. I can play with a lot of different things. You know I start editing out things more than I do adding.
I saw a video just earlier today of you and I said, "What is that keyboard in the background?" And that's probably what it was.
It's a Synclavier, yeah.
Yeah. It's got a lot of dials and buttons.
It works. It's worked since 1983.
Okay. This is my other prop, speaking of 1983.
Oh yeah.
These things were heavy.

That's a big reel too. Usually they weren't quite that big. That's almost double the amount of tape. Usually they were half that size but that wide. Yeah I mean, hey look, those days were special in lots and lots of different ways because a lot of that stuff was just being invented in a way too. It went from everyone recording live when I was a little boy in like '63 or '62. You used to have to go to another tape recorder to overdub. You would take what you had recorded on one tape recorder and do the orchestration to another tape © Fillius Jazz Archive 5
recorder, and maybe do that for the vocals and then all of a sudden your finished record had a couple generations worth of moving from one tape recorder to another.
Like The Beatles did.
Like The Beatles did. And this was prior to them doing that.

Did you find that — this is an observation again but playing the cello and then being at Curtis in ensembles, I'm guessing it must have paid off really well when you started arranging and composing, not only for the strings but just observing brass players and knowing what's capable, what's going to make them sound the best where to breathe etcetera.

You know I'm going to give you a little secret here. I was part of that Philly Sound. And what I did originally when I was little — when I was little — in my 20s I learned how these great older arrangers wrote for the MFSB which was the orchestra in Philadelphia at that time. So a lot of my initial stuff was not only my Curtis background but it was sitting there playing and listening to what they had done for the last eight years or so. And so yes it became second—hand, it became really easy for me to write because I knew what was sort of expected of the sounds of those instruments and what was expected on records. It's like you said, how do you finish a record? How do you put a proper arrangement on a record that's going to work?
Some of that is not answerable. That's what I think makes it so wonderful is that you can't pin down why things work or why some particular record that you might not even anticipate becomes a hit.

Absolutely not. But you know what a good song is, and you also know that you're not stepping on the vocalist. And you know that you're adding to the dimension of the record. That's all. But you're right. And there's no one way of doing it. There are many ways to do it.

I sometimes think of music — when you're switching radio stations for instance — you're listening to something from '58, '64, into the hip hop era. And if music was a pie chart, if the audio — to me it used to be that the vocal had the biggest slice of the pie. Now I hear bass as like the predominant thing that people hear.

Well you know what? I think it's — the record business, if you're really into the record business, is really created about through the inventions of all the technology. And what happened back in those days you couldn't really get bass to really respond enormously on the radio speaker or on these little speakers that we had. And then as — when we went to the movie theater we got bass because they had those big Voice of Music speakers that were this big. When we went to the studio we got bass because those were the same speakers that were there too. But people didn't have them in their homes. Now they've got © Fillius Jazz Archive 6

little speakers this big you have so much bass coming out of it it's incredible. So I think, and then I think that one of the things about bass — be it synth bass or regular bass — it makes the record have a lot more volume and power. So I think that's partially a lot of the reason.
I've always felt the basses can be the most important thing happening because it acts like a drum, it guides the harmony, and it takes a certain mindset to be a good and appropriate bass player.

I agree. And I agree it's one of the most important things. You know when I still get a chance to produce a whole record, when I hire — to me the bass player is the most important person I'm hiring. Because he'll drive the record, especially if it's R&B or disco or any of the kind of things that I get hired to do at this point in my life.
I pulled a quote off a shorter video that I saw of you, and you were in the studio looking at older equipment and you said, "I was hands—on back when the needs were small."
Yeah.
Do you remember saying that?
Absolutely.
Can you expand on that?

Well as I just said before this record business and the film business is based on technology. So what happens is things keep getting bigger, more complicated, it's just big. My first Neve I had was 15 channels. About this big. It was an old broadcast board. That was amazing, that I could line everything patch everything into and have everything come out of and I had a 24—track in my room in those days. Originally I had an 8— track. Okay? But eventually I had a 24—track in the room. And even though I didn't have 24 channels — I think I only had 16 — I was able to accommodate. You know? I would have the drums on a mix and I'd have this on that and everything. And it was manageable for me. I could get a record to sound the way I wanted to in my little room. Now did that translate out into the real world? I always had a professional engineer come in and mix them anyway. I did. But yes, it was much more manageable. And I still have that — well I don't have it — I sold the studio so the people who bought my studio, they still have that old Neve broadcast board.
How — in current technology where basically you have unlimited tracks and capabilities and moving things and splicing out a quarter note, is it harder to know when a song is done?

Oh yeah. Yeah you want to keep working on it. It's like, it becomes an obsession. As a matter of fact one of the things that for the last twenty years I've had the same engineer doing my strings for me and my horns for me. And a lot of times when I'm finished I © Fillius Jazz Archive 7
don't stay in the room. I let him finish it himself. Because his ears bring it to a different place than me futzing with it all the time.

Very interesting. I watched the other, this was fascinating you were in Berlin, 2018 I think, and it was a video of working with a string section and it looked like it was the first read through of what you had — I think you wrote the chart.
I didn't write the chart. I remember it.

Okay. I wonder then, because of some things you said but here's a couple of comments you made during that session to the string players. First of all, "You've got to wait." They kept coming in early on like the and of four or something, and then you said, "don't overplay" because they were just I guess really getting into it. And then you said I thought significantly, "you don't need that."

Yeah. I edited his arrangement. I went in to the control room and asked them if I could. Because they had over—written it you know? And I sort of edited it. And the string players, you know if you stayed there for an hour or two hours they would have gotten it even the way he wrote it. But the thing is why? You know? It was not necessary. So I very kindly asked him if I could edit. And he consented that. Yeah. But yeah I mean I really — you have all these microphones and you have all these things, I mean it's good to play forte all the time and show me how you can play, but the thing is is I'm more interested in the mood of the record and how the record sounds, and how the violin sounds. You know when I — or how the cello sounds. You know? I mean when I feel myself pressing either on the cello I don't like it. You know it's a tight sound. It's not an open sound. And I like an open sound. I like things to have an openness to them, in the same way that I — when I write chords I like open chords. I like — I don't like dense things. I like more things that are — it depends on the song but most of the time I like more of an open voicing.
Define — what is your version of open voicing?

My version of open voicing is almost like a string quartet. So the cello has a note, the viola has a note and the violin might have two notes or maybe three notes. It's not like eight notes. I mean there are arrangers that come in and I — the violins are stacked you know. And it's not — I'm not saying it's bad, it's just not the way I write.
Like a little air in there.
Big time. More than a little.

I think it's interesting that you talk about volume and playing really hard because you could say well play as loud as you want, we'll just pull the bar down of your volume but that's not how it works. You're still going to get loud playing softer. © Fillius Jazz Archive 8

Right. It's not the way these mics are perceived or even the way — you know one of the things about great vocalists you know they might be belters you know but they'll entice you into a song. They don't start out belting. Or some of them don't, I mean Aretha sometimes did and some of these other young people like Jennifer Hudson does sometimes. But — [there's a little traffic out here, I'm sorry]. But it's more like you're telling a story and even with your voice you're telling a story. And even with the violin or the cello or the arrangement or the record, you know it's like I remember a lot of these hip hop kids when they started coming to me in the late '90s and the middle '90s whenever it started, that big wave that I had there for a while. You know they would say after I finished an arrangement they'd say, "Man, you were like telling a story with the strings." They were the one telling the story, all I was doing was following their arc.
Following their arc. I like that.

You know and even though a lot of the hip hop records started the same and ended the same, there was always like a vocal arc. You know even the rapper had to breathe. Or on some of those records the singing came into the choruses. But I would always try to follow the arc of the song, which is what I did when I was a little kid. So to me I remember you know I mean maybe I cared too much about it but I really don't think I did. I think that part of my success within the frame of hip hop was because that's what I did.
I'm not sure what you mean, that's what you did?

I told the story with the arrangement in a way as they were telling a story, depending on what — I didn't care who it was. It could be, you know The Roots or anybody. I mean I told the story. They were telling a story and I did too. So it wasn't just the same line that came in and that's what the arranging on popular music became that. It became very similar. You'd write a line for the chorus and it came in every time.

Yeah and they wouldn't even have to play it again, we'll just like move it over there. When you were working with Gamble and Huff and Thom Bell, I'm trying to frame this idea. Before someone coined the term the Philly Sound, was there a speculation or conversations about what is Motown not doing that we could do? How can we find a niche in the market?

You know I think the big difference between Motown and Philly Sound was Motown was the sound of the young America. It was really a youth movement. R&B. Whereas the Philly sound was a sophisticated, much jazzier much more adult kind of a sound. I mean I've always thought that MFSB could have been the Lionel Hampton band. You know? And in turn, in a way, I was right. MFSB could have gone and played behind Frank Sinatra or anybody. You know? I mean it was that adept at a lot of different styles and adult styles. And I also think that, I also think Gamble, Huff and Bell, they grew up I © Fillius Jazz Archive 9

mean I think Tommy Bell was enamored with Burt Bacharach. And Burt Bacharach was very sophisticated you know? And I think a lot of Thom's arrangements back in those days were like Bacharach arrangements. They would feature a horn player or feature a flute or feature — I mean feature a harp. I mean he had his way of introducing symphonic instruments. And in the '70s, early '70s, that was a big deal I think.
Who was he writing for previous to this? Do you know?

I think that he was — I think that the main rhythm section of the Philly Sound used to work at a place called The Uptown, which was the place where all the Motown groups and all the southern groups would come in and they were the rhythm section. So they were a back—up rhythm section and I think Thom was — played piano in a whole bunch of different kinds of groups. I think as an early 20—year—old, but I think he started having hits pretty soon after that.
Do you know if he was a quote schooled musician?

He definitely went to — he went to some education yes. He had some musical education. There was a place in Philadelphia called the Combs College of Music, that was up in one of the urban neighborhoods in Philadelphia. And I think he took classes there. You know this is before, now every college has courses. You know that. I mean I have nothing to do with any universities at all but every college teaches engineering and teaches music and — in those days that wasn't the case.

Whoever wrote this promo on your website spoke about them saying, "They also had a brilliant ability to figure out what the people wanted to hear. The result? The sound of Philadelphia." How did they figure out what people wanted to hear?

Well I used to say they had the pulse. They had the beat and pulse of the neighborhoods if that makes sense. In a way it's like jazz. You know they had the beat and pulse of the neighborhoods. So to me that — my phrase that they knew what people wanted to hear, that's what I mean. And also I think if you go back and pick song to song there was a lot of like how do you say this, there was a lot of over—emotional songs that Gamble used to write. He was quite a hell of a lyricist. And some of those songs, "Me and Mrs. Jones," Billy Paul and I mean I can go on and on, but then he had another side to him where it was so commercial like "Love Train." You know that was, it was almost like what do they call those songs candy apple? I don't know the term they use in popular music.
Bubble gum.
But you know they're teenybops. You know they're like —
Yeah. Bubble gum rock.
Yeah. And Tommy Bell "La—la Means I Love You." You know? I mean just the title alone is enough to make you go oh my God. You know I remember in the early '70s my © Fillius Jazz Archive 10

wife and I were staying in New York one night. And we went into the elevator and there was an arrangement of "La—la Means I Love You." You know? Done by Muzak. And I thought to myself, "Shit this is going to really be big."
Yes if it's attracting that, those delivery system, that's a big tell. They also seem not to be afraid to write social commentary.
Big time.
Yeah. Like "Wake Up Everybody" with Harold Melvin and —

Well "Wake Up Everybody" was written by my good friend John Whitehead. That was not a Gamble song. That was McFadden and Whitehead. And John Whitehead and I were friends until he died until he got shot here in the city. But he wrote "Ain't No Stopping Us Now" which is another really big, sort of political song. And he wrote "Back Stabbers," that's a really political song. You know? I mean he was a character that kid. He was a real natural talent.
There was no discussion — or was there — about gee, this is, we can't really release this song this is too controversial?

Not for them. They were always on — black music in those days was always on the left anyway. It was never mainstream, you know? It became mainstream, you know, I mean it really did. You know by the middle '70s and the late '70s it was very mainstream to the point where MFSB went and played the White House one time, when Jimmy Carter was president. So you know Teddy Pendergrass playing the White House? You know? I mean singing at the White House? That's a little weird you know, in the '70s.
Indeed. It seems that technology and hip hop seem to go hand—in—hand with the production values. I wonder if you as a musician yourself was a bit surprised when melodic content became not necessary?

Yeah. But it was a slow ball. It wasn't like it was a fast ball. It started like in the early '80s. Late '70s already you had like the early rap songs coming out. So I knew, and then there were the DJs on the radio that all they all rhymed. Remember the old DJs? I mean the R&B DJs? They were all like poets and didn't know it. Look at Muhammad Ali. Muhammad Ali came out of that same school. Everything was a rhyme. Everything was a phrase that you could remember. So that didn't surprise me, especially being a student of black culture and black music, which I pride myself in those days. It's hard to keep up these days, at age 77. It is. I almost like want to throw my hands up a little bit. But back in those days I definitely, even in the early '80s you know there were a lot of early hip hop records that my partner and I, we worked on behind the scenes, nobody even knew.
Huh. What makes you keep going? © Fillius Jazz Archive 11

I like working, I like music, I like — been doing this since I was a little boy. It's the thing I do best actually I think. I think at this point I do this better than playing the cello even though at one time I think I played the cello better than I did this. So I think what happened was they got reversed. And I'm always fascinated, like this year I guess I can say I did a really nice song with Ed Sheeran that'll come out in September. It's like sort of like a wedding song in an R&B style and it was a good song. And I did another really nice song with — I did a couple of other songs, I can't even remember — well Bruno Mars, you know I mean I'm not even supposed to say that out loud because I signed these agreements that I'm not allowed to even talk about it. But you know these kids, some of them are really super talented songwriters, as good as all the people I used to grow up with.

I read a quote from let's see, who said it — Fred Wesley, when I spoke to him. He said this phrase probably six times in the interview talking about writing for James Brown he said, "I didn't know what I was doing." And he kept saying it, like — and I felt like saying, "Well yes you did." But have you ever been in a situation early on that you didn't feel like you knew what you were doing?

Absolutely. You learn on the job. That's what Fred means. But Fred was a great player. And he knew all about that stuff, he had grown up listening to those records. Come on. You know? But yeah I mean my early on I would look for — I would wait for Tommy Bell to smile or Gamble & Huff to say damn that's nice or McFadden and Whitehead to come in and start dancing in the studio in front of the strings. You know? All of a sudden I said, "I take it you like it." They said, "Yeah we do." I mean Whitehead used to call me the Golden Child.
Well you had no issues being accepted into that if it was a circle, but I'll call it a circle?

You know I got to, as the years went on I got more and more accepted into it. You know Kenny Gamble, I've seen him like recently and he said "Boy I wish I would have known how talented you were when we were kids." Because he thought I was just a cello player in one way. But then as the years went on he saw, and then he used to come to my studio, you know, and in one way, and then when you know his son — his son came and worked for me for a little while. Kenny called me up and said he didn't have a studio and he wasn't really into everyday record business, and he said, "My son's dying to work for someone who makes records all the time." And he came and he worked as an assistant engineer. In those days we used to have — you had to EQ the tape recorders, you had to align the tape recorders, you had to do — you know we tried to teach Caliph how to do all that and he was real happy being here. And Kenny just expressed to me the fact that he wished that he would have known the breadth of my talents back in those days. But © Fillius Jazz Archive 12

you know what? I was a shy person in a way. You know I didn't want to — I did open my mouth too much. I have to say, I wasn't that shy. But I didn't want to overstep my bounds in my relationship with Gamble, Huff and Bell.
Did you ever work with Bernard Purdie?
I worked on records that he played on, but I don't think I ever worked with him, no.
Okay. The only reason I asked is you were talking about, you know, opening your mouth maybe too often which he basically admitted to. When you —

I did — early on in the Sound of Philadelphia I would correct some of the string parts, I would if there was a wrong note here or — do this. Or tell people that, you know like you saw me do it in Berlin. I did that since I was a little boy.

I was impressed by that because not only your comments but it looked to me like those string players were very flexible because you'd say something like, "Extend that quarter note" and like I didn't see anybody frantically grabbing a pencil and, you know, it's like they were absorbing what you were saying.
Well you know after you play a song down a few times some people grab pencils and other people can remember.
Yeah. Okay.
So I mean different strokes for different folks.
Do you find that you are working on assignments even when you're not working? You go for a walk and you've still got this —

Oh yeah yeah. Especially when over the years of my lifetime I used to do my best writing when I took my power walk in the morning. You know? I would hear the song and I'd start finishing it — I'd come home, I'd grab a piece of paper and I'd start correcting what I had in my head or where I had left it the day before. Absolutely. I never thought a song was finished until I could hear it in my head completely be it in bed in the morning or, you know, I would feel much better about my arrangement if I had it that rote in me, you know, if it was that big a part of me at that moment.
What do you send in what form is your music in when you send it to your copyist?

A couple of different ways either written, either written out on the score paper, or I've used one guy who has perfect pitch and he can take my arrangement and I separate — I do the violins on the left, the violas on the right and the cello in the middle. And you know from my Synclavier he writes out my arrangements and sends me a fair copy and then I take the fair copy and I re—work that with a pencil and I work on that for a couple of days and then I call him up on Zoom and I say here are my changes and it's done.
I think it's really cool that you — a Synclavier goes back how many years now? © Fillius Jazz Archive 13
And it's still useful for you.
Big time.
Yeah.

Big time. Yeah I mean it's not state—of—the—art sound—wise at this point, you know, the way I have it. But as far as my memory and it's like a big tape recorder that I can work on parts of the song. You can do that now with computers but who wants to look at a screen all day long?
